name: Methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate
lead: Methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate (abbreviated MCE) is an organic UV filter used in sunscreens to absorb long-wave UVA radiation. According to Wikipedia it was developed by L'Oreal and BASF, and L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400, while its subsidiary La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune [1].

It has an absorption maximum at 385 nm, in the UVA1 range (360 to 400 nm) [1]. The EU approved it as a cosmetic UV filter in 2019 at up to 3%, and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration followed in 2025 at the same limit; the same page states that the US FDA does not currently recognise it [1].
No peer-reviewed clinical studies of the filter were found, and public information on its toxicology is limited to regulatory opinions and concentration caps.

paras: The compound is a yellow solid with a molar mass of about 322 g/mol and dissolves in ethanol and several cosmetic solvents [1]. Its absorption peak at 385 nm lies at the long-wave end of UVA, a region that some other filters cover less strongly [1].

The EU approval in 2019 followed an opinion of the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety, which set the 3% cap [1]. Australia approved it in 2025 at the same level [1]. According to the same source, it is used only in L'Oreal products, and it has no FDA recognition for US use [1].

The filter appears in skincare discussions mainly as an ingredient in La Roche-Posay sunscreens sold with the UVMune name, where it is mentioned as part of broad-spectrum UVA protection; no community-specific claims about it were found.

timeline.event: Approved in the EU as a cosmetic UV filter up to 3% [1]
Approved by Australia's TGA up to 3% [1]

card.summary: L'Oreal's UVA1 filter (Mexoryl 400 / UVMune), EU-approved in 2019 with no published human trials.
card.note: Not recognised by the US FDA; used only in L'Oreal-group products per Wikipedia.

quick.overview:
MCE is a newer organic UV filter that absorbs long-wave UVA (peak 385 nm). L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400, and La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune.

The EU approved it in 2019 up to 3%, and Australia in 2025. No clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVA1 radiation in the 360 to 400 nm range, with its maximum at 385 nm.
quick.risks: Public toxicology detail is limited to regulatory concentration limits. The FDA does not currently recognise it for US sunscreens.
